note: Where Scripture leaves it open whether two names are one person, or one name two people. Written with AI help and checked against the verses cited; the app marks these with the AI sparkle. Each sets out what the text says and the main ways it has been read, without choosing between them. 'people' are selectors in the same form as portraits.json.

disputes.title: Is James son of Alphaeus the same as James the brother of Jesus?
disputes.note: The apostle lists name a James son of Alphaeus (Matthew 10:3). The Gospels also name James as one of Jesus' brothers (Mark 6:3), and Mark calls a James 'the less', whose mother Mary stood at the cross (Mark 15:40). Paul meets 'James the Lord's brother' and counts him among the apostles in a broad sense (Galatians 1:19). Older Western tradition, followed by Easton's dictionary, treats all three as one man and reads 'brother' as cousin. Many modern scholars keep them apart: John 7:5 says Jesus' brothers did not yet believe in him while the Twelve were already chosen, which sits awkwardly if one of the Twelve was his brother. The text itself does not settle it.

disputes.title: Judas son of James, Thaddaeus and Lebbaeus
disputes.note: Matthew and Mark list an apostle called Thaddaeus (Mark 3:18; the King James at Matthew 10:3 reads 'Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus'). Luke and Acts have no Thaddaeus but list 'Judas the brother of James' in the same place (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13), and John mentions 'Judas, not Iscariot' (John 14:22). Most readers take these to be one apostle known by more than one name. The King James 'brother of James' supplies a word the Greek leaves out; it can equally be read 'son of James'.

disputes.title: Bartholomew and Nathanael
disputes.note: Bartholomew appears only in the lists of the Twelve, always next to Philip (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14). Nathanael appears only in John, brought to Jesus by Philip and named among the disciples at the end (John 1:45-49; 21:2). John never mentions a Bartholomew and the other Gospels never mention a Nathanael, so many have identified them, Bartholomew ('son of Tolmai') being a family name. Scripture never makes the connection itself.

disputes.title: Matthew and Levi
disputes.note: The call of the tax collector at his booth is told three times. Matthew's Gospel names him Matthew (Matthew 9:9); Mark and Luke tell the same scene and call him Levi, son of Alphaeus (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27). The stories match closely, and the lists of the Twelve include Matthew but no Levi, so he is almost universally taken to be one man with two names.

disputes.title: Mary Magdalene, Mary of Bethany and the woman who anointed Jesus
disputes.note: Luke tells of an unnamed woman, 'a sinner', who anointed Jesus' feet (Luke 7:37-38), and immediately afterwards introduces Mary Magdalene as one from whom seven devils had gone out (Luke 8:2). John names Mary of Bethany, sister of Martha and Lazarus, as the one who anointed him (John 12:3). From the late sixth century Western preaching merged all three into one penitent Magdalene. Scripture does not: it never calls Mary Magdalene a sinful woman or links her to Bethany, and most traditions now treat them as three women.

disputes.title: The women at the cross: how many, and who
disputes.note: Each Gospel names the women differently. Mark has Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses, and Salome (Mark 15:40). Matthew has Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of Zebedee's children (Matthew 27:56). John has Jesus' mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene (John 19:25). Comparing them, many conclude that Salome was the mother of James and John, and some that she was also the sister of Jesus' mother; and that 'Mary the wife of Cleophas' is the Mary mother of James and Joses. These are reasonable inferences, not statements of the text.

disputes.title: Jude who wrote the letter
disputes.note: The letter opens 'Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James' (Jude 1:1). A Judas is named among Jesus' brothers alongside James (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3), and most take the writer to be him, since a James well enough known to be named without explanation is likely the leader of the Jerusalem church. Some older writers identified him with the apostle Judas son of James instead.

disputes.title: Which Herod?
disputes.note: The New Testament calls several rulers of one family simply 'Herod'. Herod the Great reigned when Jesus was born and ordered the killing at Bethlehem (Matthew 2). His son Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, beheaded John the Baptist and questioned Jesus (Matthew 14:1-10; Luke 23:7). His grandson Herod Agrippa I killed James son of Zebedee and imprisoned Peter (Acts 12:1-3). Agrippa II heard Paul's defence (Acts 25:13-26:32). The text tells them apart by context rather than by name.

disputes.title: Who was Darius the Mede?
disputes.note: Daniel says Darius the Mede took the kingdom after Belshazzar, aged about sixty-two (Daniel 5:31; 9:1). No ruler of that name and description is known outside Daniel. Proposals include Cyrus himself under another title (Daniel 6:28 can be read 'in the reign of Darius, that is, of Cyrus'), Cyrus's general Gubaru who governed Babylon, and Cyaxares II. Others take the figure as a literary composite. The question is open.

disputes.title: Ahasuerus of Esther
disputes.note: Esther's king Ahasuerus ruled 'from India even unto Ethiopia, over an hundred and seven and twenty provinces' from Shushan (Esther 1:1-2). The Hebrew name corresponds to the Persian Khshayarsha, known in Greek as Xerxes, and most identify him with Xerxes I (486-465 BC). The Greek Septuagint calls him Artaxerxes instead. The same Hebrew name is used of other kings in Ezra 4:6 and Daniel 9:1, who are not necessarily the same man.

disputes.title: Belshazzar, 'son' of Nebuchadnezzar
disputes.note: Daniel calls Nebuchadnezzar Belshazzar's father (Daniel 5:2, 11, 18). Babylonian records show Belshazzar as the son of Nabonidus, a later king, ruling Babylon while his father was away. Many read 'father' in Daniel in the common ancient sense of predecessor or ancestor, possibly through his mother; others see it as a difficulty in the text. That Belshazzar was second in the kingdom fits his offer to make Daniel 'third ruler' (Daniel 5:16).

disputes.title: Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel
disputes.note: Ezra says Sheshbazzar, 'the prince of Judah', brought back the temple vessels and laid the foundation of the temple (Ezra 1:8; 5:16). Elsewhere Zerubbabel is the governor who laid that foundation (Ezra 3:8-10; Zechariah 4:9). Some take them to be one man with a Babylonian and a Hebrew name; others think Sheshbazzar led the first return and Zerubbabel succeeded him. Some identify Sheshbazzar with Shenazar, an uncle of Zerubbabel (1 Chronicles 3:18).

disputes.title: Which Zechariah was killed between the temple and the altar?
disputes.note: Jesus speaks of 'Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar' (Matthew 23:35). Chronicles tells of Zechariah son of Jehoiada stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:20-21), the last murder recorded in the Hebrew Bible's order, which fits 'from Abel to Zacharias'. The prophet Zechariah, however, is the son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1). Readers explain the difference as Jehoiada being a grandfather, as a copyist's addition, or as a reference to the prophet.

disputes.title: One Abimelech of Gerar, or two?
disputes.note: Abimelech king of Gerar takes Sarah, believing she is Abraham's sister (Genesis 20), and later makes a covenant with Abraham alongside his captain Phichol (Genesis 21:22). Decades on, Isaac passes Rebekah off as his sister to Abimelech king of the Philistines in Gerar, and Phichol appears again (Genesis 26). Some take this to be the same long-lived king; others think Abimelech was a royal title, like Pharaoh, borne by successive kings.

disputes.title: Which Pharaoh?
disputes.note: In Genesis and Exodus the king of Egypt is only ever 'Pharaoh', a title meaning 'great house'. Scripture distinguishes the Pharaoh of Joseph, a new king 'which knew not Joseph' who began the oppression (Exodus 1:8), and the Pharaoh of the exodus, but never names them. Proposals for the exodus king depend on the date taken for the exodus: Thutmose III or Amenhotep II for an earlier date, Ramesses II for a later one. Later Pharaohs are named: Shishak, So, Tirhakah, Necho and Hophra.

disputes.title: John Mark, Mark the Gospel writer
disputes.note: Acts names 'John, whose surname was Mark', whose mother's house was a meeting place in Jerusalem (Acts 12:12), who left Paul and Barnabas partway through their journey (Acts 13:13; 15:37-39). Paul later names Mark as Barnabas's relative (the King James says 'sister's son'; the Greek word means cousin) and calls him profitable to him (Colossians 4:10; 2 Timothy 4:11), and Peter calls him 'Marcus my son' (1 Peter 5:13). Early tradition identifies this Mark with the writer of the second Gospel, drawing on Peter's preaching. The Gospel itself does not name its author.
